# Setup

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(ggstats)
library(ggplot2)
library(jtools)
library(gtsummary)


file<-url("https://github.com/Neilblund/SDSB340-Spring-2026/raw/refs/heads/master/Data/atus.rds")
atus_fmt<-readRDS(file)

label_hours_minutes <- function(x) {
  h <- floor(x / 60)
  m <- round(x %% 60)
  
  # Logic to create strings like "1h 30m", "45m", or "2h"
  labels <- ifelse(h > 0, 
                   paste0(h, "h", ifelse(m > 0, paste0(" ", m, "m"), "")),
                   paste0(m, "m"))
  
  # Ensure NAs remain NAs
  labels[is.na(x)] <- NA
  return(labels)
}

```

### Long data

-   ggplot works best with long format data. If we want to visualize several variables at once, you'll often need to do some additional data wrangling.

### Long data

:::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

# store the variable labels in a list
labels<-lapply(atus_fmt, function(x) attr(x, "label"))|>
  unlist()
# make long format data
time_long<-atus_fmt|>
  # selecting only the weight + columns related to activities
  select(sleep:travel, TUFINLWGT)|>
  # pivoting everything except the weights
  pivot_longer(cols=-TUFINLWGT)|>
  # adding the labels as a new column
  mutate(label = labels[name])

# viewing the results
time_long|>
  slice_head(n=10)

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

time_aggregate<-time_long|>
  group_by(label)|>
  summarize(avg = weighted.mean(value, w=TUFINLWGT))
ggplot(time_aggregate, aes(x = avg, y=label)) + geom_point()



```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

time_aggregate<-time_long|>
  group_by(label)|>
  summarize(avg = weighted.mean(value, w=TUFINLWGT))|>
  mutate(label = reorder(label, avg))

ggplot(time_aggregate, aes(x = avg, y=label)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
 title = "Average time spent on different activities",    
    x = "Time spent",
    y = "",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_hours_minutes) +
  theme_bw()



```
:::
::::::

### Faceting and scaling

Big differences in the scaling can make it difficult to identify *relative* changes within each group. Faceting with "free" axes can be a useful way to highlight a change at the expense of distorting absolute values.

### Faceting and scaling

::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
This plot shows hours spent on different activities by age using the same scale for each facet.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true


time_long<-atus_fmt|>
  mutate(weekend = factor(TUDIARYDAY %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday"),
                          levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                          labels=c("Weekday", "Weekend")
                          ))|>
  select(sleep:travel, TEAGE, TUFINLWGT, weekend)|>
  pivot_longer(cols=-c(TUFINLWGT, weekend, TEAGE))|>
  mutate(label = labels[name])

time_aggregate<-time_long|>
  group_by(label, weekend, TEAGE)|>
  summarize(avg = weighted.mean(value, w=TUFINLWGT))


ggplot(time_aggregate, aes(x = TEAGE, y =avg, 
                           color=weekend,
                           group=weekend)) +
  geom_point(size=.1) +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Average time spent on different activities",    
    subtitle = "by age",
    x = "Time spent",
    y = "",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_hours_minutes) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~label,   labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 25)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 7)
        ) 
  



```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Here's what it looks like using a "free" y scale:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

time_long<-atus_fmt|>
  mutate(weekend = factor(TUDIARYDAY %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday"),
                          levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                          labels=c("Weekday", "Weekend")
                          ))|>
  select(sleep:travel, TEAGE, TUFINLWGT, weekend)|>
  pivot_longer(cols=-c(TUFINLWGT, weekend, TEAGE))|>
  mutate(label = labels[name])

time_aggregate<-time_long|>
  group_by(label, weekend, TEAGE)|>
  summarize(avg = weighted.mean(value, w=TUFINLWGT))


ggplot(time_aggregate, aes(x = TEAGE, y =avg, 
                           color=weekend,
                           group=weekend)) +
  geom_point(size=.1) +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Average time spent on different activities",    
    x = "Time spent",
    y = "",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_hours_minutes) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~label, 
             # Free scale on the y-axis
             scales='free_y',
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 30)
             ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 6)
        ) 
  



```
:::
:::::

## Survey data

Some special considerations for visualizing survey data

-   Visualizations for categorical data
-   Visualizing weighted responses
-   Handling over-plotting
-   Visualizing the margin of error
-   Visualizing the results from a model

### Survey data: Categorical Responses and Weights

-   Many survey variables are categorical rather than continuous, which can restrict our options for visualization.

#### Survey data: Bar plots

::::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
`geom_bar` automatically creates bars proportional to the number of observations.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=GTMETSTA)) + 
  geom_bar()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
`geom_col` creates bars that are proportional to a value in the data (so you need to create the aggregated data yourself)

```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(GTMETSTA)|>
  summarise(Count = n())

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=GTMETSTA, y= Count)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  theme_bw()




```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Doing the aggregation separately offers better flexibility for calculations and formatting.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(GTMETSTA)|>
  summarise(count = sum(TUFINLWGT))|>
  mutate(proportion = count /sum(count))

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=GTMETSTA, y=proportion)) + 
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Creating a dumbbell plot using `geom_pointrange` can be an appealing alternative to bar plots that focuses more attention on the important stuff (the ends)

```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(GTMETSTA)|>
  summarise(count = sum(TUFINLWGT))|>
  mutate(proportion = count /sum(count))

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=GTMETSTA, y=proportion)) + 
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = proportion),
                  # making wider lines 
                  lwd=.7, 
                  # increasing the point size
                  size = 1.5)

```
:::
:::::::

#### Survey data: Two-way bar plots

::::::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(telework, PEEDUCA)|>
  summarise(count = sum(TUFINLWGT))|>
  ungroup()|>
  drop_na()|>
  group_by(PEEDUCA)|>
  mutate(proportion = count /sum(count))

atus_agg

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
In this instance, the axis labels are too long to fit on the page.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=proportion, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  geom_col()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Using `coord_flip` (or just reversing what goes on the x and y axis) is often an easy fix in this situation.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=proportion, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Adding `position='dodge'` to the plot will give side-by-side columns, instead of stacked bars.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=proportion, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  coord_flip()+
  geom_col(position='dodge')
  

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
`scales::label_percent()` will automatically turn proportions into formatted % tick marks:

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=proportion, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent())+
  labs(x = "Education",
       y = "Percent",
       fill  = "Telework"
       )

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
You can also simplify the calculation of weighted proportions here using the `srvyr` package.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

library(srvyr)
atus_svy<-atus_fmt|>
  as_survey_design(weights = TUFINLWGT)

# getting survey proportions
atus_agg<-atus_svy|>
  # drop missing values
  drop_na(telework, PEEDUCA)|>
  # get proportions summing to 100% by education
  group_by(PEEDUCA, telework)|>
  summarise(survey_prop(vartype = 'ci'))

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=coef, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent())+
  labs(x = "Education",
       y = "Percent",
       fill  = "Telework"
       )

```
:::
:::::::::

#### Survey data: Plotting a likert-type question

Plotting Likert items can present some unique challenges. We'll walk through a couple examples for how you might create visuals for a series of agree/disagree questions.

#### Survey data: Likert Plots

Here's an example of a Likert scale plot using regular ggplot functions.




```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| 
site<-'https://github.com/Neilblund/SDSB340-Spring-2026/raw/refs/heads/master/Data/anes_tssubset.rds'
anes_subset<-readRDS(url(site))

labels<-sapply(anes_subset, function(x) attr(x, 'label'))

anes_long<-anes_subset|>
  select(id, full.weight, year, c(rr_1, rr_2, rr_3, rr_4))|>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(rr_1, rr_2, rr_3, rr_4))

anes_long$qlabel<-unlist(labels[anes_long$name])



# aggregating by year and question
summary_data<-anes_long|>
  drop_na()|>
  group_by(qlabel, value, year)|>
  summarise(n = sum(full.weight))|>
  ungroup()|>
  group_by(qlabel, year)|>
  mutate(proportion = n/sum(n),
         label = sprintf("%.0f%%",
                         proportion*100)
         )

# plotting by year and faceting by question
ggplot(summary_data, aes(x=year, y=proportion, fill=value, label=label)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size=3)+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_x_reverse()+
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_discrete(palette = "RdYlBu")  +
  labs(x = "",
       y= "%",
       fill = "",
       title = 'Racial Resentment Questions',
       caption = 'Source: ANES 2024'
  )  +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  facet_wrap(~qlabel,  labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 50))


```

#### Survey data: Likert Plots

The `gglikert` function from the `ggstats` package can produce detailed visualizations for likert type questions with minimal code. 

Note that the output produced by the `gglikert` function is still a ggplot object, so you can still add layers just like you would with other plots.


```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| echo: false



anes_subset|>
  gglikert(
    include = c(rr_1, rr_2, rr_3, rr_4),
    weights = full.weight,
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Racial resentment",
       caption = "Source: ANES Times series (1992-2024)"
       )

```



#### Survey data: Likert Plots

You don't need to pivot the data into long format for this to work, just select multiple columns in the "include" argument.

```{r}
#| output-location: column



anes_subset|>
  gglikert(
    include = c(rr_1, rr_2, rr_3, rr_4),
    weights = full.weight,
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Racial resentment",
       caption = "Source: ANES Times series (1992-2024)"
       )

```

#### Survey data: Likert Plots

The `facet_rows` and `facet_cols` arguments will produce faceted output:

```{r}
#| output-location: column

anes_subset|>
  filter(year %in%c(2000, 2024))|>
  gglikert(
    include = c(rr_1, rr_2, rr_3, rr_4),
    weights = full.weight,
    facet_rows = vars(year)
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Racial resentment by year",
       caption = "Source: ANES Times series (2000 vs. 2024)"
       
       )
```  

#### Survey data: Likert Plots

If the goal is to show change over time, it might make sense to draw plots separately for each question so that the results for each year are easier to compare.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

# alternatively: looking at a single question over a longer period of time

anes_subset|>
  gglikert(
    include = rr_2,
    facet_rows = vars(year),
    weights = full.weight,
    variable_labels=c(rr_2 = "")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Agree/Disagree: \"Blacks should not have special favors to succeed\"" ,
       caption = "Source: ANES Times series (1992-2024)"
       
  )


```


### Overplotting


### Handling overplotting

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Over-plotting occurs when data points or labels overlap. This happens a lot with survey variables that only have a few discrete values.


:::
  
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=TRERNWA/100, y=sports_recreation )) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Example of overplotting",
       x = "Weekly Wages",
       y="Time spent on sports and recreation"
  )


```
:::
:::::


#### Handling overplotting

Some options

:::: r-stack

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}

Using a different shape or size (ex: `pch=21` will give hollow circles)
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}

Changing the transparency level (adjusting `alpha` to a value less than 1 will make transparent points)
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}

Adding random noise with a "jitter" (take note of whether you need more noise on the X or Y axis)
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4}
Hexbin plots "bin" the data into groups and then use color-coding to indicate the number of observations in each bin (like a histogram in 2-dimensions)

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5}
2D density plots are analogous to a kernel density plot.

:::
::::


:::: r-stack

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=0}

```{r}
#| output-location: column



ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=TRERNWA/100, y=food )) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Example of overplotting",
       x = "Weekly Wages",
       y="Time spent on eating and drinking"
  )


```

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=TRERNWA/100, y=food )) + 
  geom_point(pch=21) + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Example of overplotting",
       x = "Weekly Wages",
       y="Time spent on eating and drinking"
  )


```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=TRERNWA/100, y=food )) + 
  geom_point(alpha=.3) + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Example of overplotting",
       x = "Weekly Wages",
       y="Time spent on eating and drinking"
  )


```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=TRERNWA/100, y=food )) + 
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(height=5, width=0)) + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Example of overplotting",
       x = "Weekly Wages",
       y="Time spent on eating and drinking"
  )


```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=TRERNWA/100, y=food )) + 
  geom_hex(bins=60) + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Example of overplotting",
       x = "Weekly Wages",

```
:::

ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=TRERNWA/100, y=food)) +

  theme_bw() +

  ) +

#### Handling overplotting

When all else fails, you might consider making one of the variables discrete and then use a box plot or strip chart to visualize the relationship of interest.


```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_fmt|>
  mutate(income_discrete = factor(ntile(TRERNWA/100, 10))
         )|>
  drop_na(income_discrete)|>
ggplot(aes(x=income_discrete, y=food)) + 
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width=.2, height=0), alpha=.3, pch = 21) +
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE, alpha=.8, fill='orange') + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Example of overplotting",
       x = "Weekly Wages (decile)",
       y="Time spent on eating and drinking"
  ) +
  coord_flip()
```

### Visualizing Uncertainty and Model Results

How should we visualize an estimate with uncertainty?

```{r}
#| output-location: column

yngchild<-atus_fmt|>
  filter(TRYHHCHILD < 5)|>
  droplevels()

yngchild |>
  tbl_summary(
    include = hh_caretaking,
    by = TESEX,
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"
  ) |>
  add_ci()

```


#### Visualizing Uncertainty

`stat_summary` functions can be used to compute both a mean and a confidence interval for the same value:



:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}

```{r}
#| output-location: column


ggplot(yngchild, aes(x = TESEX, y = hh_caretaking)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, 
               geom = "point",
               size = 3, 
               color = "red") +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(x= "Sex", 
       y="Time spent caring for household members")

    

```

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
```{r}
#| output-location: column


ggplot(yngchild, aes(x = TESEX, y = hh_caretaking)) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               geom = "errorbar",
               width = 0.2) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    size = 3,
    color = "red"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Sex", 
       y = "Time spent caring for household members")

    

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}
```{r}
#| output-location: column


ggplot(yngchild, aes(x = TESEX, y = hh_caretaking)) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = ~ sample_frac(.x, 0.20),
    alpha = .3,
    width = .05,
    height = 1,
    pch = 21
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               geom = "errorbar",
               width = 0.2) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    size = 3,
    color = "red"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "Time spent caring for household members")

    

```
:::


::::


#### Visualizing Uncertainty


Keep in mind that sample size impacts the width of your confidence intervals. So you might prefer to combine similar groups to improve statistical power.



:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}


```{r}
#| output-location: column


yngchild |>
  ggplot(aes(x = TRSPPRES, y = hh_caretaking)) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               geom = "errorbar",
               width = 0.2) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    size = 3,
    color = "red"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Cohabitation", 
       y = "Time spent caring for household members") +
  coord_flip()

    

```

    


:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

yngchild$cohab<-fct_collapse(
  yngchild$TRSPPRES, 
  `Spouse or partner present` = c("Unmarried partner present", "Spouse present"))

yngchild |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cohab, y = hh_caretaking)) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               geom = "errorbar",
               width = 0.2,) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    size = 3,
    color = 'red'
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Cohabitation", 
       y = "Time spent caring for household members") +
  
  coord_flip()

```
:::

#### Visualizing Model Results:  Regression

- Regression models give the effect of a one unit increase in one or more independent variables on the expected value of some outcome variable. 

- They're a useful way to show the association between two variables while controlling for some third (or fourth or fifth additional characteristic)

#### Visualizing Model Results:  Regression


![](images/reg_results.png)
from: Campos N, Federico C. A New Measure of Affective Polarization. American Political Science Review. 2026;120(1):160-178. doi:10.1017/S0003055425000255

#### Visualizing Model Results:  Regression


```{r}


model<-lm(hh_caretaking ~ TESEX + cohab + TRYHHCHILD , data=yngchild )
# getting formatted regression output:
tbl_regression(model)

```




#### Visualizing Model Results

:::: {.r-stack}



::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
```{r}
#| output-location: column


effect_plot(model, pred='TESEX') +
  labs(x = "Sex", 
       y = "Time spent on caretaking",
       title  ='Predicted time spent on caretaking by sex')

```

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}

#### Visualizing Uncertainty



```{r}
atus_fmt|>
  filter(TRYHHCHILD < 5)|>
  ggplot(aes(x=TESEX, y=hh_caretaking, weight= TUFINLWGT)) + 
  geom_point(position=position_jitter(width = .2), alpha=.5, pch=21) + 
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE , alpha=.6) + 
  theme_bw()

```

### General tips on data visualization
  
  -   The best way to learn is through replication: find an example and adapt it. [here's a great place to start](https://r-graph-gallery.com/)

-   Care.

-   Consider resolution and audience: slide decks should have big plots with minimal detail, written reports can tolerate more subtlety.

-   Almost all "3d" plots are pointless.
